label: Incidence Problems
notes: This chapter runs across printed pages 41 to 76 and asks one deceptively simple question: how many times can points and lines touch. We will see that combinatorial geometry answers it sharply with the Szemeredi-Trotter theorem, and that a graph-drawing invariant supplies the cleanest proof known.

label: Counting Incidences
notes: An incidence is just a flag, a point lying on a line. The incidence count I of m points and n lines is the size of this relation. The whole subject is bounding this single integer, because so many distance and pattern questions reduce to counting incidences between geometric objects.

label: Easy Bounds
notes: Two lines meet in at most one point, so no two points share two common lines. A Cauchy-Schwarz double count on this constraint already yields an incidence bound of order m times root n plus n. It is correct in spirit but far from tight, which motivates the deeper theorem.

label: Szemeredi-Trotter
notes: The Szemeredi-Trotter theorem states the true maximum: incidences are of order m to the two-thirds times n to the two-thirds, plus m plus n. This bound is tight, matched by a grid construction, and it is the central result of the chapter and the engine for everything downstream.

label: Tightness: The Grid
notes: A square root-m by root-m integer grid with lines of small rational slope realizes the extremal count. Checking that the two-thirds exponents are achieved convinces us the theorem cannot be improved. The grid is the canonical witness that the upper bound is best possible up to constants.

label: Crossing Number
notes: The crossing number of a graph is the fewest pairwise edge crossings over all drawings in the plane. Planar graphs have crossing number zero and obey Euler's bound of at most three n minus six edges. Forcing more edges forces crossings, and quantifying that pressure is the key idea.

label: Crossing Number Inequality
notes: When a graph has at least four times as many edges as vertices, its crossing number is at least e cubed over sixty-four n squared. The proof deletes random vertices, applies the linear Euler bound to the survivor, and optimizes the sampling probability. This cubic lower bound is the whole trick.

label: Proof of Szemeredi-Trotter
notes: Build a graph whose vertices are the points and whose edges join consecutive points along each line. Edge count is incidences minus lines. The crossings are bounded by pairs of lines, so the crossing inequality squeezes incidences from above and delivers the two-thirds exponents almost mechanically.

label: Unit Distances
notes: How many pairs of n points can be exactly distance one apart. Replacing each point by a unit circle turns unit-distance pairs into point-circle incidences. Two circles meet twice, mimicking the two-line rule, so the Szemeredi-Trotter machinery yields an n to the four-thirds upper bound.

label: Distinct Distances
notes: Dually, n points must determine many distinct distances. A counting argument against the unit-distance bound forces at least order root n distinct distances, far from the near-linear truth later proved by Guth and Katz. The gap shows how incidence bounds both enable and limit distance geometry.

label: Incidences with Curves
notes: The same scheme generalizes to circles and bounded-degree curves. When any two curves meet in at most a constant number of points, a crossing-number drawing again applies and produces Szemeredi-Trotter-type bounds, though the exponents weaken with the multiplicity of intersections allowed between curves.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We counted incidences, proved the tight Szemeredi-Trotter bound through the crossing-number inequality, and harvested unit-distance, distinct-distance, and curve applications. The takeaway is a method: translate a geometric extremal question into a graph drawing and let the crossing invariant do the counting.
